pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Logs, metrics, traces: what question is each one best at answering, and what does it cost you to lean on the wrong one?
expected_points: metrics: how much/how often/how slow over time, cheap pre-aggregated numbers, cost is the number of time series
traces: where the time went across services/hops, cost is sampling
logs: what exactly happened in one request, highest detail, cost is volume and retention
they overlap badly: counting log lines instead of a counter is expensive and slow to query; averages cannot give you a p99

questions.prompt: Walk me through your ContextHandler: what does Handle do, why does WithAttrs have to re-wrap, and how does the level get changed while the process runs?
expected_points: Handle reads the ids off the ctx of the logging call and adds request_id / trace_id / span_id to the record, then delegates
WithAttrs/WithGroup return a Handler; returning the embedded one strips the decorator so every derived logger loses the ids
the JSON handler is configured with a slog.Leveler — a *slog.LevelVar can be Set at runtime, no redeploy
attrs are typed key/values, not interpolated into the message

questions.prompt: Pick the metric type for each of these and say why: requests served, requests currently in flight, request latency. Why does a counter panic on a negative delta in your registry?
expected_points: counter for requests served — you read its rate, not its value
gauge for in-flight — goes up and down
histogram for latency — cumulative buckets plus sum and count, so quantiles are computable without storing every observation
rates assume monotonicity; a decrease is read as a process restart, so a decrementable counter corrupts every query built on it

questions.prompt: Why is the route label `/items/{id}` rather than the actual path, and what happens if you add a user_id label instead?
expected_points: each distinct label combination is its own time series, and combinations multiply
unbounded values (paths with ids, user ids, error strings) explode series count and can take the monitoring system down during an incident
labels must be bounded and known in advance; high-cardinality detail belongs in logs and traces
the route is only known after the mux matched, hence the route holder on the context

questions.prompt: A request arrives with a traceparent header and your handler calls another service. Trace the ids through: what do you read, what do you create, what do you send, and what do you do with a malformed header?
expected_points: parse traceparent: version, 32-hex trace id, 16-hex span id, flags (sampling bit)
create a new span: same trace id, new span id, parent = the incoming span id; put it on the context
outbound calls inject the current span context back into a traceparent header, which is what joins the two services' spans into one trace
a malformed header is rejected and a fresh trace starts — never let a caller's garbage corrupt yours
context.Context is the carrier so deep call sites do not need extra parameters

questions.prompt: Your p99 latency alert fires. Which signal do you open first, and how do you get from the alert to the line of code?
expected_points: metrics first: they are what the alert is built on; narrow by route, status, instance, and check rate vs duration vs saturation
traces next to localize which hop or dependency owns the time
logs last, filtered by the trace id of a slow request, to explain why
profiling (pprof) if the time is inside this process
correlation works because request_id and trace_id are on every log record

questions.prompt: What is the difference between /healthz and /readyz, and what goes wrong if a liveness check pings the database?
expected_points: liveness answers 'is this process broken' and a failure gets it killed and restarted, so it must check nothing external
readiness answers 'should this instance get traffic now' and a failure only removes it from the load balancer
a liveness check on the database turns a blip into a fleet-wide restart storm that hammers the recovering dependency
readiness names the failing check, and failing it first is how you drain traffic before graceful shutdown

questions.prompt: Your dashboard averages the p99 latency across ten instances. What is wrong with that number, and how accurate is any single p99 from your histogram?
expected_points: percentiles do not average — you aggregate the bucket counts and then compute the quantile
a histogram quantile is interpolated within a bucket, so its precision depends on where you put the bucket boundaries
choose buckets around the latencies in your SLO

questions.prompt: You wrote a registry and a tracer by hand. Name what OpenTelemetry calls each piece you built, then say what you would replace with a library at work and what you would keep.
expected_points: the mapping: SpanContext is otel's SpanContext, Tracer.Start/Span.End are its Tracer and Span, ParseTraceparent + Inject are a propagator (propagation.TraceContext), Finished stands in for an exporter
replace the registry with prometheus/client_golang and the tracer with OpenTelemetry (API + SDK + exporter, usually a collector)
keep the handler decorator, the middleware order, the route holder, the health/readiness split — those are design, not plumbing
the exposition format, get-or-create registration, cumulative buckets and traceparent parsing are no longer magic, which is what makes the libraries' knobs legible
